opus-5.5.text:
So, I think the motivation was pretty simple. If you're worried about alignment, one of the most basic problems is that we train systems to do what looks good to a human evaluator, and that works reasonably well as long as the human can tell what's good. RLHF was in some sense the most straightforward version of that: take the thing that we'd naively do, actually do it, and see where it breaks. I thought it was important to have that baseline working in practice, both so we'd understand its failure modes empirically and so the more ambitious work, like trying to scale oversight beyond what humans can directly evaluate, would have something concrete to build on.

There was also a sociological piece. I think it's healthy for alignment research to be connected to systems people actually deploy. If your safety techniques only exist on paper, it's hard to know whether they work, and it's hard to get people building AI to take them seriously. Having a technique that's actually useful made it more likely that labs would invest in this kind of work, and that alignment would be seen as part of building AI rather than a separate, speculative thing.

Now, I do think there's a real cost there, and I've gone back and forth on how big it is. RLHF made models more useful, and that probably increased interest and investment in AI, which plausibly sped things up somewhat. My overall take is that the effect was modest. Something like RLHF was very likely to be developed soon anyway because it's so commercially obvious, and the benefits, getting experience with the technique, understanding where it fails, building a research community around these problems, seem to me to outweigh that. But I don't think it's crazy to see it differently, and I take that consideration seriously when thinking about what to work on next.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that I never thought of RLHF as a solution to alignment. It's more like the starting point. The core problem is still there: once models are doing things humans can't easily evaluate, optimizing for human approval can get you behavior that looks good rather than behavior that is good. A lot of what I've cared about since then is figuring out how to deal with that gap.

r001.rationale: The response says having RLHF working in practice gives more ambitious alignment research, such as scaling oversight, something concrete to build on.

r002.rationale: It describes RLHF as a straightforward approach to try in practice so researchers could see where it breaks and learn its failure modes empirically.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there are a couple of different things going on there. One is that when I started working on RLHF, around 2016, 2017, the basic motivation was pretty simple: we're going to have systems that are increasingly capable, and the way we train them today is by writing down an objective and optimizing it. And for a lot of the tasks we actually care about, you can't write down the objective. You can't write a reward function for "be a helpful assistant" or "summarize this document well." So the natural question is, okay, if a human can recognize good behavior but can't specify it, can we just have the human evaluate the behavior and train on that signal? That's the whole idea. It's not a deep idea. It was more like the obvious first thing to try, and the surprising part was that nobody had really done it seriously at scale with modern deep learning systems.

And I think the reason I was interested in it, from an alignment perspective, is that I viewed it as sort of the baseline. Like, if you want to understand how hard alignment is, you want to start with the simplest plausible approach and see where it breaks. And RLHF is the simplest plausible approach. The failure modes are also pretty clear in advance. If the human can't tell whether the output is good, then you're training the model to produce things that look good to the human, which is not the same as things that are good. That gap is the thing I've spent most of my career worrying about. So in some sense the point of working on RLHF was partly to get the thing working so that we'd then be confronting the real problem, which is what you do when the human evaluator is no longer competent to judge.

The other thing I'd say is that I didn't anticipate how commercially important it would end up being. I think at the time it felt like a fairly niche research direction. The fact that it became the thing that made language models usable as products was not really part of the plan. And I have mixed feelings about that. On one hand, I think it's good that the labs deploying these systems are using methods that at least try to make them do what people want, rather than just maximizing next-token likelihood. On the other hand, you could argue that making the systems more useful accelerated the whole field, and I'm not sure that's net positive. I don't think RLHF specifically is responsible for most of that acceleration, but I take seriously the possibility that work that's framed as safety work ends up mostly being capabilities work in disguise.

So when I think about whether it was the right call, I mostly land on yes, but not with huge confidence. I think the version of the world where nobody worked on this and labs were deploying raw pretrained models with prompt hacking would be worse. And I think the research community understands the limitations of RLHF much better now because people actually tried it, rather than just theorizing about it. But I also think RLHF is pretty clearly not the thing that gets us all the way. It's a stepping stone, and the real work is figuring out what comes after it when humans can't supervise directly anymore.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF was a baseline for testing alignment and a stepping stone toward harder problems, but does not argue that accelerating concrete developments is valuable to researchers pursuing speculative AI ideas.

r002.rationale: The response calls RLHF a simple approach and notes that trying it helped the community understand its limitations, but it does not clearly say that simple-seeming methods reveal many problems in practice.

astra-6.text:
I think I was mostly coming at it from the other direction: what’s a problem that we need to solve for alignment, and can we find a version of it that we can study empirically today? We want to train AI systems to do things that are hard to specify with a simple reward function. Human feedback is a natural starting point for that.

The fact that it has practical applications is helpful because you get people working on it, you get experience with what actually goes wrong, and you can test your ideas on increasingly capable systems. But it also creates a tension, because making systems more useful is not the same as making progress on the parts of alignment that will ultimately be hardest.

So I wouldn’t take the commercial success of RLHF as evidence that we’ve solved alignment. The question I care about is what happens when the system can do things that humans can’t easily evaluate. Can we still provide feedback that rewards actually doing a good job, rather than just producing something that looks good to us? I see RLHF as a starting point for studying that problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are two different questions. One is whether you can make an AI system do things that people actually want, in cases where people can recognize a good answer. The other is whether you can extend that to cases where the AI understands what’s going on much better than the person giving feedback. I was mostly interested in the second question, but RLHF seemed like a natural place to start.

If you want to study how to train systems using human judgments, it helps to have a setup where those judgments actually improve the system. You can learn what goes wrong, what kinds of feedback are useful, and how the model generalizes. And there’s a pretty direct path from that to questions like: can we use AI assistance to help humans evaluate things they couldn’t evaluate on their own?

The fact that it had near-term applications was a mixed bag. It made it much easier to get people to work on it and to get empirical evidence. But making AI systems more useful also helps accelerate their deployment. So I wouldn’t regard adoption of RLHF, by itself, as a safety success. The thing I ultimately care about is whether we can make the training signal remain meaningful as systems become more capable than the people supervising them.

r001.rationale: The candidate says RLHF was a natural starting point for the harder question and that its near-term applications made it easier to attract researchers and get empirical evidence, connecting practical work to more speculative AI research.

r002.rationale: The candidate says studying human-judgment training can reveal what goes wrong, but does not say that methods that seem simple on paper can expose many problems in practice.
